summary:
Muğla, the province containing Bodrum, Marmaris and Fethiye, stands under the national framework of Turkey. Turkey has permitted transgender people to change their legal gender since 1988, but only on condition of sex-reassignment surgery, a medical examination and court permission. Turkish marriage law determines eligibility by the gender recorded in a person's civil registry rather than by trans status, so a visitor who has legally changed registered gender may marry a partner of the opposite registered gender. Same-sex marriage, civil unions and adoption are not available in Turkey, and no comprehensive law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. When the 12th judicial reform package passed in 2026, provisions discriminating against LGBTQ people were removed from the bill, though it made symbolic same-sex weddings possible that carry no legal marital status.

No region-specific signal was identified for Muğla itself. The enforcement patterns documented nationally reach resort-province institutions like Muğla's: authorities regularly and arbitrarily ban events by LGBT groups, local authorities around the country have increasingly cancelled concerts by artists openly supportive of LGBT rights, and the TV regulator RTÜK has justified fines on digital platforms for LGBT-related content as violating 'societal and cultural values.' These patterns colour what any visible LGBT assembly in Muğla can expect.
tangentialFactors: HRW's World Report 2024, covering 2023, records that the Erdoğan government made anti-LGBT hate speech a core part of its election campaign, and that the ninth successive ban on Istanbul Pride week events in June was accompanied by police arrests of those who attempted to assemble. Istanbul is a separate province; the ban is cited here as evidence of the national enforcement climate a visitor to Muğla would also stand under.
localsOnly: Residents of Muğla seeking to change registered gender must undergo sex-reassignment surgery, a medical examination and court permission. There is no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and same-sex marriage, civil unions and adoption are unavailable. Local authorities around the country have increasingly cancelled concerts by artists openly supportive of LGBT rights, a practice that applies to Muğla's institutions as well.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the national criminalisation package referenced in the parent framework has since passed remains unresolved in the sources. The 12th judicial reform package's removal of discriminatory provisions is reported as of 2026; its interaction with any pending criminalisation package is not sourced here.

No Muğla-specific incidents, detentions, bans or institutional practices were identified in the inventory; the enforcement patterns cited are national in scope.
